description:
Somos 4 estudiantes con perfiles diferentes pero una misma curiosidad: construir tecnología para explorar más allá de la Tierra.

Combinamos desarrollo, datos, IA, diseño y visión de producto para transformar problemas complejos en soluciones intuitivas. Un equipo preparado para explorar, analizar y construir.
summary: LUNARA is an interactive lunar south-pole mission-planning prototype designed to help users understand and compare the environmental challenges of potential landing sites. By combining NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, lunar geometry and selected terrain-derived horizon profiles, LUNARA estimates Sun and Earth visibility, illumination opportunities, solar-array output and direct-to-Earth communication windows. Its interactive 2D and 3D visualisations, mission timelines and scenario comparisons turn complex astronomical data into information that is easier to explore and interpret. Built with Python, SpiceyPy, JavaScript and Three.js, LUNARA connects scientific data processing with accessible mission-planning tools. Our goal is to make early lunar site assessments clearer, faster and easier to communicate.
details:
THE CHALLENGE: PLANNING A MISSION AT THE LUNAR SOUTH POLE

The Moon may look like a predictable environment, but its south pole presents some of the most demanding conditions for future surface missions.

In this region, sunlight often remains close to the horizon. Mountains and crater rims can block illumination for extended periods, while the Earth can disappear below the local horizon, interrupting direct communication with mission control.

These conditions create two fundamental operational challenges: **generating enough solar power and maintaining contact with Earth.**

Small changes in landing location or mission date can significantly affect both. When launch delays or hardware constraints force mission planners to reconsider their original plans, they need to evaluate alternative sites and timelines quickly.

We developed LUNARA to make these environmental constraints easier to explore, understand and compare.

Figure 1. LUNARA's main mission-planning workspace, combining site configuration, 3D lunar visualisation and environmental indicators.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES LUNARA DO?

1. Mission scenario configuration

Users can choose predefined reference sites, including the Shackleton region, Apollo 11, Mount Huygens and Marius Hills, or enter custom planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude and altitude.

Mission start and end times are configurable in UTC. Users can also adjust the analysis duration and temporal resolution.

2. Visualise the local environment in 3D

The Local Sky view shows the Sun and Earth relative to the selected site's local horizon. Users can interact with the scene to understand the geometry of the surrounding lunar environment.

The Lunar Location view provides a global 3D representation of the Moon with the selected site marked.

Figure 2. Local Sky 3D: the solar panel, lunar horizon and relative position of Earth from the selected landing site.

3. Monitor Sun and Earth geometry

Quick-read cards and detailed telemetry display elevation, azimuth, geometric visibility, visible time, peak elevation and predicted horizon crossings.

The Environment Timeline plots how the elevation of the Sun and Earth changes throughout the selected mission window. Opportunity Windows highlight periods when the solar disk or Earth's disk is geometrically visible.


Figure 3. Solar Environment and Earth Geometry telemetry, with elevation curves and predicted visibility windows.

4. Estimate solar power opportunities

LUNARA includes a configurable flat solar-panel model. Users can change panel tilt, azimuth and efficiency to estimate incident solar irradiance in W/m².

This provides a first-order indication of how the local solar geometry affects potential power generation.

5. Assess direct-to-Earth communication opportunities

Maintaining contact with Earth is another critical constraint for lunar surface operations.

LUNARA combines Earth visibility from the selected lunar site with visibility from NASA's three Deep Space Network complexes: Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra.

The communications module estimates direct-to-Earth opportunities and provides an idealised radio link-budget calculation for configurable radio bands and antenna systems. It also estimates round-trip signal propagation delay using the Earth–Moon distance.

Figure 4. Link to Earth: visualising the Moon–Earth geometry and the visibility of the three DSN ground complexes.

6. Compare mission scenarios

Users can compare up to three site-and-date combinations using key indicators such as total solar visibility, Earth visibility and peak estimated solar output.

Results can be exported as CSV files, making comparisons easier to document and share.

7. Explore annual environmental patterns with Surface Map

Surface Map provides a regional view of the lunar south pole by displaying the share of time that the Sun or Earth remains above the local terrain over a one-year analysis window.

Users can switch between two map layers:

  • Sunlight: maps the percentage of the analysis period during which the Sun is visible above the local terrain.
  • Earth in view: maps the percentage of the analysis period during which Earth is visible above the local terrain.

Figure 5. Annual sunlight availability across the lunar south polar region, showing the percentage of the selected one-year window during which the Sun is visible above local terrain.Figure 6. Annual Earth visibility across the lunar south polar region, showing how terrain and geometry influence potential direct-to-Earth visibility.

8. Explore potential landing locations

Candidate Explorer helps users investigate alternative locations across the lunar polar region.

Users configure minimum visibility requirements and geographic screening parameters, including:

  • Minimum hours with the Sun's centre visible.
  • Minimum hours with Earth's disk visible.
  • Northern latitude limit.
  • Coordinate-grid spacing.

The tool scans a coordinate grid and ranks candidate locations according to the selected geometric conditions. Results display planetocentric coordinates, altitude, estimated Sun visibility and Earth visibility.

Users can then load a candidate directly into the main Observatory to investigate its environmental conditions in greater detail.

Figure 7. Candidate Explorer: preliminary screening of lunar polar locations against configurable visibility thresholds

HOW DOES IT WORK?

LUNARA combines scientific data processing in Python with a browser-based JavaScript geometry and visualisation engine.

STEP 1. Ephemeris generation — Knowing where the Sun and Earth are

A Python script using SpiceyPy relies on NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels to precompute the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the Moon, expressed in the Moon's body-fixed IAU_MOON reference frame.

The resulting time-series data is stored in JSON format. The application interpolates between available samples to obtain positions at the selected time, without extrapolating beyond the dataset's coverage.

STEP 2. Local geometry — Turning positions into a local sky

The JavaScript engine interpolates between available ephemeris samples and transforms the Moon-relative position vectors into a local East-North-Up coordinate frame at the selected site.

This makes it possible to calculate the local elevation and azimuth of the Sun and Earth, determine geometric visibility and identify horizon crossings.

No extrapolation is performed beyond the available ephemeris coverage.

STEP 3. Terrain awareness — Accounting for the lunar landscape

For selected catalogue locations, LUNARA uses precomputed local horizon profiles derived from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data.

These azimuth-dependent horizon masks account for terrain obstructions without requiring the full elevation dataset to be loaded in the browser.

Where no local terrain profile is available, the application uses an idealised tangential horizon. These results are preliminary and should not be interpreted as terrain-validated predictions.

STEP 4. Solar power estimation — Understanding illumination

Solar irradiance is projected onto a configurable flat panel using its tilt, azimuth and efficiency.

The resulting value provides a first-order estimate of available solar power per unit area, helping users compare different illumination conditions and panel orientations.

STEP 5. Communications analysis — Maintaining contact with Earth

Direct-to-Earth opportunities are estimated by combining the visibility of Earth from the lunar site with the visibility of the Moon from the Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra DSN complexes.

The model considers the Moon visible above a 10° elevation threshold at a ground station and calculates an idealised communication link budget using free-space path loss, antenna gain, system noise and a 3 dB margin.

Earth–Moon distance is also used to estimate signal propagation delay.

STEP 6. Interactive visualisation — Making complex information accessible

The browser interface brings these calculations together through interactive charts, timelines, comparison tables and Three.js-powered 3D views.

The result is a workspace where users can explore environmental conditions and compare mission scenarios without having to interpret raw ephemeris vectors themselves.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

For mission planners and engineering teams

  • Quickly assess the environmental conditions of candidate sites and dates.
  • Understand how changing a landing date or location can affect solar illumination and communication opportunities.
  • Compare scenarios when launch delays or mission constraints require alternative plans.
  • Bring lighting, terrain-related horizon information and communications considerations into a shared workspace.

For educators and the public

  • Make the unusual lighting conditions of the lunar south pole easier to understand.
  • Visualise why the Sun and Earth can disappear below the local horizon.
  • Explore the scientific and engineering challenges involved in planning lunar surface operations.

Our Intended Impact

LUNARA aims to bridge the gap between complex scientific datasets and accessible mission-planning visualisation. By making environmental constraints easier to understand and compare, we hope to support early-stage lunar site trade studies and improve the communication of mission-planning decisions across scientific and engineering disciplines.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

LUNARA combines web development, scientific computing and astronomical data processing.

Frontend and visualisation

  • HTML5 — application structure.
  • CSS3 — interface styling and responsive presentation.
  • JavaScript — geometry calculations, data processing and interactive behaviour.
  • Three.js (v0.160.0) — interactive 3D lunar and spatial visualisations.

Scientific computing and backend

  • Python — ephemeris preprocessing and the local SPICE service.
  • NumPy — numerical operations and scientific data handling.
  • SpiceyPy — Python interface to the SPICE toolkit.

Scientific data and reference systems

  • NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels — planetary ephemerides, leap seconds and lunar body-fixed reference frame constants.
  • IAU_MOON — Moon-fixed coordinate reference frame.
  • NASA LRO LOLA elevation data — source for selected local terrain-horizon profiles.
  • NASA Deep Space Network information — ground communication complex references.

Deployment and accessibility

The main interface runs in a web browser. No dedicated hardware is required. Precomputed ephemeris data can be loaded by the browser application, while the real-SPICE workflow uses the local Python service.

LIMITATIONS AND SCIENTIFIC SCOPE

LUNARA is a research and visualisation prototype intended for preliminary geometric assessments. It is not a certified landing-site selection, flight dynamics or spacecraft engineering system.

Ephemeris and geometry: Results depend on the time coverage and resolution of the loaded SPICE dataset. Interpolation is performed within the available dataset, with no extrapolation beyond its coverage.

Terrain: LOLA-derived local horizon profiles are currently available for selected catalogue locations. Other candidate-grid results use an idealised flat-horizon screening and have not been validated against local terrain. The 3D terrain representation is illustrative rather than a certified topographic mesh.

Solar power: The irradiance model projects sunlight onto a configurable flat panel. It does not include thermal behaviour, dust accumulation, panel degradation, lander self-shadowing or electrical power-system losses. It should therefore be interpreted as an indicative estimate, not a complete power-system simulation.

Communications: The communications module uses a simplified lunar visibility model and an idealised link budget. The current implementation does not model atmospheric or rain fade, pointing and polarisation losses, DSN scheduling or relay satellites. Its lunar ephemeris for ground-station visibility is low precision (approximately 0.2°).

Thermal conditions: The application does not currently calculate precise lunar surface temperatures or provide a validated thermal model.

We consider transparent communication of these assumptions essential to responsible scientific visualisation.

RESOURCES AND SCIENTIFIC FOUNDATIONS

The project draws on NASA/JPL scientific data and openly documented scientific computing and visualisation resources.

Its principal scientific foundations are NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides for solar and Earth geometry, the IAU_MOON reference frame, and LRO LOLA elevation products for selected terrain-aware horizon profiles.

NASA's Deep Space Network provides the reference for the three ground communication complexes. NASA SVS and Solar System Scope provide visual texture resources for the 3D presentation.

The corresponding datasets, software libraries and source links are listed in the dedicated NASA Data and Space Agency Partner & Other Data sections of this submission.

NEXT STEPS - BEYOND THE PROTOTYPE

LUNARA is a first step towards a more complete lunar mission-planning workspace. Our next development priorities are:

01. Full LOLA terrain integration

Extend the use of real lunar elevation data into horizon calculations and the Candidate Explorer. This will allow a broader range of candidate locations to be assessed with terrain-aware visibility rather than preliminary flat-horizon assumptions.

02. A more complete solar power model

Develop the current first-order irradiance estimate into a more representative power assessment, incorporating additional operational factors such as thermal behaviour, dust, degradation, lander shadows and electrical-system effects.

03. Improved mission assessment

Continue refining the comparison workflow, scientific model transparency and environmental analysis so that users can better understand the consequences of changing mission locations and timelines.

OUR VISION

The next lunar mission will face decisions that begin long before landing. LUNARA aims to make those decisions easier to explore, compare and communicate, bringing scientific data one step closer to practical mission planning.

FIND THE RIGHT PLACE. FIND THE RIGHT TIME.
